name: Ingrid Solberg
headline: 34, owner of a smoked-fish company, Bergen
title: Harbor Invitation
situation: On a Saturday afternoon, Ingrid is at the harbor picking up a fresh batch of ice for the smokehouse. Lars, an old friend from her dock days, calls out and walks over. He's smiling, a bit gray in the beard, and says a few of their old group are meeting at his boat later for coffee and fresh herring. He knows she's busy but tells her it's been two years. Ingrid's truck is loaded, and her checklist for the evening is already set. She pauses, the salt air mixing with the smell of her own smoked fish, and considers saying yes or making her usual excuses.

context.relationship_profiles:
Lars is the one old dock friend who still treats her as Ingrid rather than 'the Solberg girl'; they have traded favors since shared tuna-rigging seasons, but there is no standing obligation between them.
The rest of the old group has drifted to Christmas cards and the occasional funeral, so he is the keeper of their shared history.
context.tendencies:
She has cancelled the last three proposed gatherings with the same excuse—smokehouse scheduling—and once mailed a smoked salmon box as an apology.
On the rare occasions she has said yes, she has arrived late and left within ninety minutes, checklist in hand.
context.current_state:
She has been up since 4 AM testing brine batches and the evening re-smoke order is already written on her clipboard.
Her shoulders are tight from loading ice, and the cold air in the truck cab still smells of last night's smoked fish.
context.immediate_memories:
The fresh herring calls up a July afternoon on her father's fjord cruiser when she first filleted a mackerel under his exacting gaze.
Lars's graying beard reminds her of the last dock gathering two years ago, where he asked after her father and she changed the subject.
The salt smell carries the memory of watching the boat she sold being towed away, the engine bolt still in her palm.
context.reflective_memories:
Her grandmother's ledger discipline tells her a national title is won the same way a season's pack is—without coffee interruptions.
But her father used to say that a crew that shares herring becomes a crew worth trusting, and she has heard that phrase return to her more often lately.
She has also noticed over the years that every time she lets the group go, a little more of the Ingrid who fished for fun slips away.
